theory.title: Test Templates for Data-Driven Testing
theory.content:
## What is Data-Driven Testing?

Data-driven testing is a methodology where you execute the **same test logic** with **different input data**, verifying that the system behaves correctly across various scenarios. Instead of writing separate tests for each data set, you define the test logic once and feed it multiple data sets.

### Traditional Approach vs. Data-Driven

**Traditional (repetitive):**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Password Length Test 1
    ${length}    Get Length    password123
    Should Be Equal    ${length}    ${11}

Password Length Test 2
    ${length}    Get Length    secret
    Should Be Equal    ${length}    ${6}

Password Length Test 3
    ${length}    Get Length    myp@ssw0rd
    Should Be Equal    ${length}    ${10}
```

**Data-driven (template-based):**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Password Tests
    [Template]    Check Password Strength
    password123    ${11}
    secret         ${6}
    myp@ssw0rd     ${10}

*** Keywords ***
Check Password Strength
    [Arguments]    ${password}    ${expected}
    ${length}    Get Length    ${password}
    Should Be Equal    ${length}    ${expected}
```

**Benefits:**
- Less code duplication
- Easier to add new test cases (just add data row)
- Centralized test logic
- Clearer separation of test logic vs. test data

## Test Templates in Robot Framework

The `[Template]` setting transforms a test case into a **data-driven test**. Each subsequent line in the test case becomes a **separate execution** of the template keyword with different arguments.

### Basic Template Syntax

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test Name
    [Template]    Keyword Name
    arg1    arg2    arg3
    arg1    arg2    arg3
    arg1    arg2    arg3
```

Each data row is executed independently, and failures in one row don't prevent others from running.

### How Templates Work

**Under the hood:**
```robot
Password Tests
    [Template]    Check Password Strength
    password123    ${11}
    secret         ${6}
```

Is equivalent to:
```robot
Password Tests - Row 1
    Check Password Strength    password123    ${11}

Password Tests - Row 2
    Check Password Strength    secret    ${6}
```

Robot Framework executes each row as a **sub-test** within the parent test case.

### Template Execution and Reporting

**Pass/fail behavior:**
- Each data row is executed independently
- If one row fails, others still execute
- Test case passes only if **all rows pass**
- Reports show individual row results

**Example output:**
```
Password Tests                                          | PASS |
  password123, 11                                       | PASS |
  secret, 6                                             | PASS |
  myp@ssw0rd, 10                                        | PASS |
```

If one row fails:
```
Password Tests                                          | FAIL |
  password123, 11                                       | PASS |
  secret, 5                                             | FAIL |
  myp@ssw0rd, 10                                        | PASS |
```

## Building Template Keywords

Template keywords must accept **arguments** matching the data row structure.

### Simple Template Keyword

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Check Password Strength
    [Arguments]    ${password}    ${expected}
    ${length}    Get Length    ${password}
    Should Be Equal    ${length}    ${expected}
```

**Structure:**
1. `[Arguments]` defines expected parameters
2. Test logic operates on the arguments
3. Assertion validates expected outcome

### Complex Template Keywords

Templates can invoke multiple steps:

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Validate Login
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}    ${expected_status}
    Open Browser       https://app.com    Chrome
    Input Text         id:username        ${username}
    Input Text         id:password        ${password}
    Click Button       id:login
    Page Should Contain    ${expected_status}
    [Teardown]         Close Browser
```

Usage:
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Login Tests
    [Template]    Validate Login
    admin        admin123    Dashboard
    user1        pass456     Dashboard
    invalid      wrong       Invalid credentials
```

## When to Use Templates

### Good Use Cases

**1. Validation scenarios:**
```robot
Email Validation
    [Template]    Validate Email Format
    user@example.com         Valid
    invalid.email            Invalid
    @example.com             Invalid
    user@domain              Invalid
```

**2. Calculation testing:**
```robot
Math Operations
    [Template]    Verify Addition
    2     3     5
    10    5     15
    -2    2     0
```

**3. Boundary testing:**
```robot
Age Validation
    [Template]    Validate Age Range
    0      Invalid
    17     Invalid
    18     Valid
    65     Valid
    150    Invalid
```

**4. Cross-browser/platform testing:**
```robot
Browser Compatibility
    [Template]    Test Login On Browser
    Chrome
    Firefox
    Edge
    Safari
```

### When NOT to Use Templates

**1. Tests with different logic:**
If each scenario requires unique steps, separate test cases are better.

**2. Complex setup requirements:**
If each data set needs different preconditions, templates become awkward.

**3. Few data variations:**
For 1-2 data sets, traditional test cases are simpler.

## Advanced Template Features

### Default Template (Suite Level)

```robot
*** Settings ***
Test Template    Check Password Strength

*** Test Cases ***
Password 1
    password123    ${11}

Password 2
    secret    ${6}
```

All test cases in the suite use the same template unless overridden.

### Embedded Arguments in Templates

```robot
*** Keywords ***
User ${username} should have role ${role}
    [Arguments]    # No explicit arguments needed
    ${actual_role}    Get User Role    ${username}
    Should Be Equal    ${actual_role}    ${role}

*** Test Cases ***
Role Validation
    [Template]    User ${username} should have role ${role}
    admin     administrator
    user1     standard
    guest     visitor
```

### Combining Templates with Tags

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Critical Validations
    [Template]    Validate Email Format
    [Tags]        critical    smoke
    admin@company.com    Valid
    ceo@company.com      Valid
```

## Get Length Keyword

The `Get Length` keyword (from BuiltIn library) returns the number of items in strings, lists, or dictionaries.

**For strings:**
```robot
${len}    Get Length    Hello        # Returns 5
${len}    Get Length    password123  # Returns 11
```

**For lists:**
```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
${len}      Get Length     ${items}    # Returns 3
```

**For dictionaries:**
```robot
&{user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30
${len}     Get Length           ${user}      # Returns 2
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Descriptive Data

Make data rows self-documenting:

```robot
# Poor: Magic numbers
    password123    11

# Better: Clear values
    password123    ${11}    # Expected length
```

### 2. Consistent Argument Order

Keep argument order logical:
- Inputs first, expected outputs last
- `Check Password Strength    ${password}    ${expected_length}`

### 3. Handle Edge Cases

Include boundary and error cases:

```robot
Password Tests
    [Template]    Check Password Strength
    ${EMPTY}         ${0}     # Empty string
    a                ${1}     # Single character
    ${'x' * 100}     ${100}   # Very long password
```

### 4. Use Variables for Test Data

```robot
*** Variables ***
${SHORT_PASS}     abc
${MEDIUM_PASS}    password123
${LONG_PASS}      VeryLongPassword123!

*** Test Cases ***
Password Tests
    [Template]    Check Password Strength
    ${SHORT_PASS}     ${3}
    ${MEDIUM_PASS}    ${11}
    ${LONG_PASS}      ${20}
```

By mastering test templates, you can efficiently test multiple scenarios, improve coverage, and maintain cleaner test suites.
learningObjectives: Understand data-driven testing principles and benefits
Use [Template] setting to create data-driven test cases
Build template keywords that accept multiple argument sets
Recognize when templates improve test efficiency and maintainability

theory.title: Managing Test Data with Variables Section
theory.content:
## Centralizing Test Data

The `*** Variables ***` section is Robot Framework's mechanism for **centralizing test data** and **configuration values** in one location. This promotes **maintainability** by separating data from logic and enables easy updates without modifying test code.

### Why Variables Section?

**Without Variables section:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test 1
    Login    admin    admin123
    Verify Role    administrator

Test 2
    Login    user1    pass456
    Verify Role    standard

Test 3
    Login    guest    guest789
    Verify Role    visitor
```

Problems:
- Test data scattered throughout tests
- Hard to update (e.g., changing usernames)
- Difficult to see all test data at once

**With Variables section:**
```robot
*** Variables ***
@{USERS}    admin    user1    guest
@{PASSWORDS}    admin123    pass456    guest789
@{ROLES}    administrator    standard    visitor

*** Test Cases ***
Test All Users
    FOR    ${i}    IN RANGE    3
        Login    ${USERS}[${i}]    ${PASSWORDS}[${i}]
        Verify Role    ${ROLES}[${i}]
    END
```

Benefits:
- All test data in one place
- Easy to modify values
- Clear data overview
- Reusable across tests

## List Variables

List variables (`@{NAME}`) store **ordered collections** of values.

### Defining Lists

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{USERS}        admin    user1    guest
@{BROWSERS}     Chrome   Firefox  Edge
@{NUMBERS}      1        2        3        4        5
```

**Syntax rules:**
- Name starts with `@{` and ends with `}`
- Items separated by **4+ spaces** (or 2+ minimum)
- Can contain strings, numbers, or variables

### Using Lists

**Access individual items (0-indexed):**
```robot
Log    ${USERS}[0]      # Logs: admin
Log    ${USERS}[1]      # Logs: user1
Log    ${USERS}[2]      # Logs: guest
```

**Iterate with FOR loop:**
```robot
FOR    ${user}    IN    @{USERS}
    Log    ${user}
END
```

Output:
```
admin
user1
guest
```

**Pass entire list to keyword:**
```robot
Log Many    @{USERS}    # Logs all items
Should Contain    @{USERS}    admin
```

**Get list length:**
```robot
${count}    Get Length    ${USERS}
Should Be Equal    ${count}    ${3}
```

### Creating Lists at Runtime

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Dynamic List
    @{items}    Create List    apple    banana    cherry
    Append To List    ${items}    date
    ${length}    Get Length    ${items}
    Should Be Equal    ${length}    ${4}
```

## Scalar Variables

Scalar variables (`${NAME}`) store **single values**.

```robot
*** Variables ***
${APP_NAME}      MyApp
${BASE_URL}      https://example.com
${TIMEOUT}       30
${ADMIN_EMAIL}   admin@example.com
```

**Usage:**
```robot
Log    Application: ${APP_NAME}
Open Browser    ${BASE_URL}    Chrome
Set Selenium Timeout    ${TIMEOUT}
```

## Dictionary Variables

Dictionary variables (`&{NAME}`) store **key-value pairs**.

```robot
*** Variables ***
&{ADMIN}     username=admin    password=admin123    role=administrator
&{CONFIG}    api_key=abc123    timeout=30           retry_count=3
```

**Access values:**
```robot
Log    ${ADMIN.username}      # Logs: admin
Log    ${ADMIN.password}      # Logs: admin123
Log    ${ADMIN}[role]         # Logs: administrator (alternative syntax)
```

**Usage in keywords:**
```robot
Login    ${ADMIN.username}    ${ADMIN.password}
```

## FOR Loop Iteration

FOR loops iterate over collections, executing the same logic for each item.

### Basic FOR Loop with List

```robot
FOR    ${user}    IN    @{USERS}
    Log    Processing user: ${user}
END
```

**Syntax:**
- `FOR` keyword starts the loop
- `${variable}` holds current item
- `IN` separates variable from collection
- `@{list}` expands to list items
- Loop body indented with 4 spaces
- `END` terminates the loop

### FOR Loop with Inline Values

```robot
FOR    ${browser}    IN    Chrome    Firefox    Edge
    Open Browser    https://example.com    ${browser}
    Close Browser
END
```

### FOR Loop with Range

```robot
FOR    ${i}    IN RANGE    5
    Log    Iteration ${i}
END
```

Output:
```
Iteration 0
Iteration 1
Iteration 2
Iteration 3
Iteration 4
```

### FOR Loop with Index

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{USERS}    admin    user1    guest
@{ROLES}    administrator    standard    visitor

*** Test Cases ***
Test With Index
    FOR    ${i}    IN RANGE    ${USERS.__len__()}
        Log    User ${USERS}[${i}] has role ${ROLES}[${i}]
    END
```

Better approach using `Enumerate`:
```robot
${pairs}    Evaluate    list(zip($USERS, $ROLES))
FOR    ${user}    ${role}    IN    @{pairs}
    Log    User ${user} has role ${role}
END
```

## Combining Variables and Loops

### Example: User Validation

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{USERS}           admin    user1    guest
@{EXPECTED_ROLES}  administrator    standard    visitor

*** Test Cases ***
Validate All User Roles
    FOR    ${user}    IN    @{USERS}
        ${role}    Get User Role    ${user}
        Log    ${user} has role: ${role}
    END
```

### Example: Multi-Browser Testing

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{BROWSERS}    Chrome    Firefox    Edge
${URL}         https://example.com

*** Test Cases ***
Test On All Browsers
    FOR    ${browser}    IN    @{BROWSERS}
        Open Browser    ${URL}    ${browser}
        Page Should Contain    Welcome
        [Teardown]    Close Browser
    END
```

## Variable Scope

Variables in `*** Variables ***` section have **suite scope**:
- Available in all test cases in the suite
- Available in all keywords in the suite
- Available in imported resource files (if referenced)

**Suite-level variables:**
```robot
*** Variables ***
${SHARED_VALUE}    100

*** Test Cases ***
Test 1
    Log    ${SHARED_VALUE}    # Works

Test 2
    Log    ${SHARED_VALUE}    # Works
```

**Test-level variables (not shared):**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test 1
    ${local}    Set Variable    Local value
    Log    ${local}    # Works

Test 2
    Log    ${local}    # FAILS - variable not defined
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Use Descriptive Names

```robot
# Poor
@{L1}    a    b    c

# Good
@{VALID_USERNAMES}    alice    bob    charlie
```

### 2. Group Related Variables

```robot
*** Variables ***
# User credentials
${ADMIN_USER}    admin@example.com
${ADMIN_PASS}    admin123

# API configuration
${API_URL}       https://api.example.com
${API_KEY}       abc123
${API_TIMEOUT}   30

# Test data
@{TEST_USERS}    user1    user2    user3
```

### 3. Use UPPERCASE for Constants

```robot
${BASE_URL}        https://example.com
${DEFAULT_TIMEOUT} 30
@{SUPPORTED_BROWSERS}    Chrome    Firefox
```

### 4. Separate Data from Logic

Keep test data in Variables section, test logic in Test Cases/Keywords.

### 5. Consider Variable Files for Large Datasets

```robot
*** Settings ***
Variables    test_data.py
Variables    config.yaml

*** Test Cases ***
Test With External Data
    Log    ${USERNAME}    # From test_data.py
```

**test_data.py:**
```python
USERNAME = "admin"
PASSWORD = "admin123"
USERS = ["alice", "bob", "charlie"]
```

By leveraging the Variables section and list iteration, you create **data-driven, maintainable tests** that are easy to update and extend.
learningObjectives: Define list, scalar, and dictionary variables in Variables section
Use list variables to store collections of test data
Iterate over lists using FOR loops
Apply variable scoping rules (suite vs. test level)

theory.title: Parameterized Test Cases and Reusable Keywords
theory.content:
## Parameterization in Testing

Parameterized test cases use **reusable keywords** with different **argument values** to test multiple scenarios. Unlike templates (which run many data rows in one test), parameterized tests create **separate, named test cases** that share the same logic but use different inputs.

### Templates vs. Parameterized Tests

**Template approach (data-driven, single test):**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Calculation Tests
    [Template]    Verify Calculation
    1    2    3
    5    7    12
    10   10   20
```

**Parameterized approach (multiple tests):**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Add 1 and 2
    Verify Calculation    1    2    3

Add 5 and 7
    Verify Calculation    5    7    12

Add 10 and 10
    Verify Calculation    10    10    20
```

**Comparison:**

| Aspect | Templates | Parameterized Tests |
|--------|-----------|--------------------|
| Test count | 1 test, multiple rows | Multiple distinct tests |
| Test names | Auto-generated (row data) | Explicit, descriptive |
| Failure isolation | Rows independent | Tests independent |
| Readability | Compact, data-focused | Verbose, scenario-focused |
| Best for | Large datasets (10+ cases) | Few scenarios (2-10 cases) |

## Creating Parameterized Keywords

Parameterized keywords accept **arguments** and perform operations based on those inputs.

### Basic Parameterized Keyword

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Verify Calculation
    [Arguments]    ${a}    ${b}    ${expected}
    ${result}    Evaluate    ${a} + ${b}
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    ${expected}
```

**Structure:**
1. `[Arguments]` defines input parameters
2. Logic operates on arguments
3. Assertion validates expected outcome

### Using the Keyword

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Add 1 and 2
    Verify Calculation    1    2    3

Add 5 and 7
    Verify Calculation    5    7    12
```

Each test:
- Has a **descriptive name** explaining the scenario
- Calls the **same keyword** with different values
- Appears as a **separate test** in reports
- Can have **different tags, documentation, or setup**

## When to Use Parameterized Tests

### Good Use Cases

**1. Few distinct scenarios (2-10 tests):**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Valid Email Format
    Validate Email    user@example.com    Valid

Invalid Email Missing At
    Validate Email    userexample.com    Invalid

Invalid Email Missing Domain
    Validate Email    user@    Invalid
```

Each test has a clear, descriptive name explaining what's being validated.

**2. Scenarios with different meanings:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Admin Can Delete Users
    Test Permission    admin    delete_user    Allowed

Standard User Cannot Delete Users
    Test Permission    user    delete_user    Denied

Guest Cannot Access Admin Panel
    Test Permission    guest    access_admin    Denied
```

Each scenario represents a **distinct business rule** worth naming explicitly.

**3. Different setup/teardown needs:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test On Chrome
    [Setup]    Open Browser    ${URL}    Chrome
    Verify Homepage
    [Teardown]    Close Browser

Test On Firefox
    [Setup]    Open Browser    ${URL}    Firefox
    Verify Homepage
    [Teardown]    Close Browser
```

### When to Use Templates Instead

**Large datasets:**
```robot
# Better as template (20+ test cases)
Password Validation
    [Template]    Validate Password Strength
    password123    Weak
    secret         Weak
    P@ssw0rd!      Strong
    # ... 17 more cases
```

**Pure data validation:**
```robot
# Better as template (repetitive data checks)
Number Range Tests
    [Template]    Verify In Range
    5     1    10    True
    0     1    10    False
    10    1    10    True
    11    1    10    False
```

## Benefits of Parameterized Tests

### 1. Descriptive Test Names

**Template (auto-generated names):**
```
Calculation Tests                                 | PASS |
  1, 2, 3                                         | PASS |
  5, 7, 12                                        | PASS |
```

**Parameterized (explicit names):**
```
Add 1 and 2                                       | PASS |
Add 5 and 7                                       | PASS |
Add Two Negative Numbers                          | PASS |
```

Clearer intent and easier to understand failures.

### 2. Test-Specific Configuration

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Critical Calculation - Add 1 and 2
    [Documentation]    Verifies basic addition (critical path)
    [Tags]    critical    smoke
    Verify Calculation    1    2    3

Edge Case - Add Negative Numbers
    [Documentation]    Tests handling of negative values
    [Tags]    edge-case
    Verify Calculation    -5    -3    -8
```

Each test can have unique documentation and tags.

### 3. Independent Test Execution

```bash
# Run specific test by name
robot --test "Add 1 and 2" tests.robot

# Run tests matching pattern
robot --test "Add*" tests.robot
```

Easier to target specific scenarios.

## Advanced Parameterization Patterns

### Multiple Keywords Per Test

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Complete User Workflow
    Create User       testuser    password123
    Verify User Exists    testuser
    Login User        testuser    password123
    Verify Dashboard Visible
    Delete User       testuser

*** Keywords ***
Create User
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}
    # Implementation

Verify User Exists
    [Arguments]    ${username}
    # Implementation
```

### Nested Keyword Calls

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Test User Workflow
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}    ${role}
    Create User      ${username}    ${password}
    Assign Role      ${username}    ${role}
    Verify Access    ${username}    ${role}

*** Test Cases ***
Admin Workflow
    Test User Workflow    admin    pass123    administrator

Standard User Workflow
    Test User Workflow    user1    pass456    standard
```

### Combining with Variables

```robot
*** Variables ***
${USER1}      alice
${USER2}      bob
${ADMIN}      admin

*** Test Cases ***
Test User 1
    Verify User    ${USER1}

Test User 2
    Verify User    ${USER2}

Test Admin
    Verify User    ${ADMIN}
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Clear Test Names

```robot
# Poor: Generic names
Test 1
    Verify Calculation    1    2    3

Test 2
    Verify Calculation    5    7    12

# Good: Descriptive names
Add Two Positive Numbers
    Verify Calculation    1    2    3

Add Two Larger Numbers
    Verify Calculation    5    7    12
```

### 2. Consistent Keyword Arguments

Keep argument order logical:
- **Inputs first:** `${a}`, `${b}`
- **Expected outputs last:** `${expected}`

```robot
Verify Calculation
    [Arguments]    ${a}    ${b}    ${expected}    # Good order
```

### 3. Reusable Keywords

Design keywords to be broadly applicable:

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Verify Calculation
    [Arguments]    ${a}    ${b}    ${expected}
    ${result}    Evaluate    ${a} + ${b}
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${result}    ${expected}
```

Can be used for addition, but could be generalized:

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Verify Math Operation
    [Arguments]    ${operation}    ${a}    ${b}    ${expected}
    ${result}    Evaluate    ${a} ${operation} ${b}
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${result}    ${expected}

*** Test Cases ***
Test Addition
    Verify Math Operation    +    1    2    3

Test Subtraction
    Verify Math Operation    -    5    3    2
```

### 4. DRY Principle (Don't Repeat Yourself)

If you copy-paste test steps, extract to a keyword:

```robot
# Before (repetitive)
*** Test Cases ***
Test 1
    Open Browser    ${URL}    Chrome
    Login    user1    pass1
    Verify Dashboard
    Close Browser

Test 2
    Open Browser    ${URL}    Chrome
    Login    user2    pass2
    Verify Dashboard
    Close Browser

# After (parameterized keyword)
*** Test Cases ***
Test User 1
    Test Login Workflow    user1    pass1

Test User 2
    Test Login Workflow    user2    pass2

*** Keywords ***
Test Login Workflow
    [Arguments]    ${username}    ${password}
    Open Browser    ${URL}    Chrome
    Login    ${username}    ${password}
    Verify Dashboard
    [Teardown]    Close Browser
```

By mastering parameterized test cases, you create **readable, maintainable test suites** that balance code reuse with clear test intent.
learningObjectives: Create reusable keywords with arguments for parameterized testing
Write multiple test cases that share logic but use different data
Understand when to use parameterized tests vs. templates
Apply DRY principle to avoid test code duplication

theory.title: List-Based Data Validation Patterns
theory.content:
## Dynamic List Creation and Validation

While the `*** Variables ***` section defines **static test data**, many test scenarios require **runtime list creation** and validation. The `Create List` keyword from the BuiltIn library enables creating lists dynamically during test execution.

### Static vs. Dynamic Lists

**Static (Variables section):**
```robot
*** Variables ***
@{NUMBERS}    2    4    6    8

*** Test Cases ***
Validate Numbers
    FOR    ${num}    IN    @{NUMBERS}
        Should Be True    ${num} > 0
    END
```

**Dynamic (runtime creation):**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Numbers
    ${numbers}    Create List    2    4    6    8
    FOR    ${num}    IN    @{numbers}
        Should Be True    ${num} > 0
    END
```

**When to use each:**
- **Static:** Test data known in advance, reused across tests
- **Dynamic:** Data calculated at runtime, test-specific values

## Create List Keyword

The `Create List` keyword creates a list variable from arguments.

### Syntax

```robot
${list}    Create List    item1    item2    item3
```

**Returns:** A list variable containing all arguments

### Examples

```robot
# Simple list
${numbers}    Create List    1    2    3    4    5

# Mixed types
${mixed}      Create List    Hello    42    ${TRUE}    ${user}

# Empty list
${empty}      Create List

# List from variables
${names}      Create List    ${first_name}    ${last_name}
```

### Dynamic List Building

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Build Dynamic List
    ${items}    Create List
    Append To List    ${items}    First
    Append To List    ${items}    Second
    ${len}    Get Length    ${items}
    Should Be Equal    ${len}    ${2}
```

## Should Be True Keyword

The `Should Be True` keyword evaluates **Python expressions** and fails if the result is not truthy.

### Syntax

```robot
Should Be True    expression
Should Be True    expression    Custom error message
```

**Expression:** Any Python expression returning True/False

### Examples

**Numeric comparisons:**
```robot
Should Be True    5 > 3
Should Be True    ${age} >= 18
Should Be True    ${count} < 100
Should Be True    ${price} == 9.99
Should Be True    ${x} != ${y}
```

**String checks:**
```robot
Should Be True    '${name}' == 'Alice'
Should Be True    len('${password}') >= 8
Should Be True    '${email}'.endswith('@example.com')
```

**Boolean values:**
```robot
Should Be True    ${is_active}
Should Be True    ${enabled} == ${TRUE}
Should Be True    not ${is_locked}
```

**Complex expressions:**
```robot
Should Be True    ${age} >= 18 and ${age} <= 65
Should Be True    ${score} > 60 or ${extra_credit} == ${TRUE}
```

### Custom Error Messages

```robot
Should Be True    ${age} >= 18    User must be 18 or older
Should Be True    ${balance} > 0    Account balance must be positive
```

When assertion fails, the custom message is displayed.

## Validating Lists with FOR Loops

Combining `FOR` loops with `Should Be True` enables **batch validation** of list items.

### Basic Pattern

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate All Positive
    ${numbers}    Create List    2    4    6    8
    FOR    ${num}    IN    @{numbers}
        Should Be True    ${num} > 0
    END
```

**How it works:**
1. Create list with values to validate
2. Loop through each item
3. Assert condition for each item
4. If any assertion fails, test fails

### Validation Patterns

**All items meet condition:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
All Even Numbers
    ${numbers}    Create List    2    4    6    8    10
    FOR    ${num}    IN    @{numbers}
        Should Be True    ${num} % 2 == 0    ${num} is not even
    END
```

**Range validation:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
All Within Range
    ${ages}    Create List    25    30    45    60
    FOR    ${age}    IN    @{ages}
        Should Be True    ${age} >= 18 and ${age} <= 65
    END
```

**String validation:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
All Valid Emails
    ${emails}    Create List    alice@example.com    bob@test.org
    FOR    ${email}    IN    @{emails}
        Should Be True    '@' in '${email}'
    END
```

**Length validation:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
All Passwords Strong
    ${passwords}    Create List    P@ssw0rd!    MyS3cr3t    Str0ng#Pass
    FOR    ${pwd}    IN    @{passwords}
        Should Be True    len('${pwd}') >= 8
    END
```

## Advanced Validation Techniques

### Validation with Index

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Ordered List
    ${numbers}    Create List    1    2    3    4    5
    FOR    ${i}    IN RANGE    ${numbers.__len__()}
        ${num}    Set Variable    ${numbers}[${i}]
        Should Be True    ${num} == ${i} + 1
    END
```

### Validation with Counter

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Count Valid Items
    ${numbers}    Create List    -2    4    -6    8    10
    ${valid_count}    Set Variable    ${0}
    FOR    ${num}    IN    @{numbers}
        ${is_positive}    Evaluate    ${num} > 0
        ${valid_count}    Set Variable If    ${is_positive}    ${valid_count + 1}    ${valid_count}
    END
    Should Be Equal    ${valid_count}    ${3}
```

### Validation with Collections Library

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    Collections

*** Test Cases ***
Validate List Contents
    ${numbers}    Create List    2    4    6    8
    List Should Contain Value    ${numbers}    4
    List Should Not Contain Value    ${numbers}    5
    ${length}    Get Length    ${numbers}
    Should Be Equal    ${length}    ${4}
```

## Real-World Use Cases

### API Response Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate API Response IDs
    ${response}    GET    /api/users
    ${ids}         Get From Dictionary    ${response}    user_ids
    FOR    ${id}    IN    @{ids}
        Should Be True    ${id} > 0
        Should Be True    isinstance(${id}, int)
    END
```

### UI Element Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate All Links Are Visible
    @{links}    Get WebElements    css:a.nav-link
    FOR    ${link}    IN    @{links}
        Element Should Be Visible    ${link}
        ${href}    Get Element Attribute    ${link}    href
        Should Be True    '${href}'.startswith('http')
    END
```

### Data Quality Checks

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Customer Ages
    ${ages}    Query Database    SELECT age FROM customers
    FOR    ${age}    IN    @{ages}
        Should Be True    ${age} >= 0    Age cannot be negative
        Should Be True    ${age} <= 150   Age unrealistic
    END
```

### File Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Log Files
    @{files}    List Files In Directory    /var/log
    FOR    ${file}    IN    @{files}
        Should Be True    '${file}'.endswith('.log')
        ${size}    Get File Size    /var/log/${file}
        Should Be True    ${size} > 0
    END
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Clear Failure Messages

```robot
# Poor: Generic error
Should Be True    ${age} >= 18

# Good: Specific error
Should Be True    ${age} >= 18    User age ${age} must be 18 or older
```

### 2. Early Failure Detection

```robot
# Fail fast if list is empty
${numbers}    Create List    2    4    6    8
${count}      Get Length    ${numbers}
Should Be True    ${count} > 0    No numbers to validate
FOR    ${num}    IN    @{numbers}
    Should Be True    ${num} > 0
END
```

### 3. Use Appropriate Assertion Keywords

```robot
# Instead of Should Be True for equality
Should Be True    ${x} == 5

# Use Should Be Equal
Should Be Equal    ${x}    ${5}
```

### 4. Log Validation Progress

```robot
FOR    ${num}    IN    @{numbers}
    Log    Validating number: ${num}
    Should Be True    ${num} > 0
END
```

By combining dynamic list creation, FOR loops, and conditional assertions, you can validate complex data structures and collections efficiently in your Robot Framework tests.
learningObjectives: Create lists dynamically at runtime using Create List keyword
Use Should Be True to evaluate conditional expressions
Validate multiple values efficiently using FOR loops
Apply data validation patterns to real-world test scenarios
relatedConcepts: Assertion keywords (Should Be Equal, Should Contain, etc.)
Conditional validation with Run Keyword If

theory.title: Dictionary-Based Data Validation
theory.content:
## Dictionaries for Structured Data

Dictionaries (also called maps or hash tables) store **key-value pairs**, making them ideal for representing **structured data** like user profiles, configuration settings, API responses, or database records.

### Why Dictionaries?

**Without dictionaries (separate variables):**
```robot
${user_name}     John
${user_age}      30
${user_role}     admin
${user_email}    john@example.com
```

Problems:
- No logical grouping
- Hard to pass related data together
- Variable naming complexity

**With dictionaries:**
```robot
&{user}    name=John    age=30    role=admin    email=john@example.com
```

Benefits:
- **Logical grouping:** Related data in one structure
- **Easy access:** `${user.name}`, `${user.age}`
- **Passing to keywords:** Send entire object
- **Mirrors real data:** JSON, database rows, API responses

## Collections Library

The `Collections` library provides keywords for working with lists and dictionaries beyond the BuiltIn library's capabilities.

### Importing Collections

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    Collections
```

**Key dictionary keywords:**
- `Create Dictionary` - Create dictionary from key=value pairs
- `Get From Dictionary` - Retrieve value by key
- `Set To Dictionary` - Add/update key-value pairs
- `Dictionary Should Contain Key` - Assert key exists
- `Dictionary Should Contain Value` - Assert value exists
- `Get Dictionary Keys` - Get all keys as list
- `Get Dictionary Values` - Get all values as list

## Create Dictionary Keyword

The `Create Dictionary` keyword creates a dictionary from key=value arguments.

### Syntax

```robot
${dict}    Create Dictionary    key1=value1    key2=value2    key3=value3
```

### Examples

**User profile:**
```robot
${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    role=admin
```

**API configuration:**
```robot
${config}    Create Dictionary    api_key=abc123    timeout=30    retry_count=3
```

**Mixed types:**
```robot
${data}    Create Dictionary    count=${42}    active=${TRUE}    name=Test
```

**Empty dictionary:**
```robot
${empty}    Create Dictionary
```

## Accessing Dictionary Values

### Dot Notation (Direct Access)

```robot
&{user}    name=John    age=30    role=admin
Log    ${user.name}     # Logs: John
Log    ${user.age}      # Logs: 30
Log    ${user.role}     # Logs: admin
```

**Limitations:**
- Only works with `&{dict}` variables from Variables section
- Keys must be valid Python identifiers (no spaces or special chars)

### Get From Dictionary Keyword

```robot
${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    role=admin
${name}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    name
Log    ${name}    # Logs: John
```

**Advantages:**
- Works with `${dict}` variables created at runtime
- Supports any key name (including spaces)
- Can provide default values

**With default value:**
```robot
${status}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    status    default=active
```

### Bracket Notation (Advanced)

```robot
${name}    Set Variable    ${user}[name]
```

Similar to Python dictionary access.

## Validating Dictionary Data

### Individual Field Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate User Data
    ${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    role=admin
    
    # Validate role
    ${role}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    role
    Should Be Equal    ${role}    admin
    
    # Validate age
    ${age}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    age
    Should Be True    ${age} > 18
    
    # Validate name exists
    ${name}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    name
    Should Not Be Empty    ${name}
```

### Using Dictionary Assertion Keywords

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    Collections

*** Test Cases ***
Validate User Structure
    ${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    role=admin
    
    # Assert keys exist
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${user}    name
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${user}    age
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${user}    role
    
    # Assert specific values
    Dictionary Should Contain Value    ${user}    admin
    
    # Get and validate
    ${role}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    role
    Should Be Equal    ${role}    admin
```

## Real-World Use Cases

### API Response Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate API User Response
    ${response}    GET    /api/users/123
    ${user}        Convert To Dictionary    ${response.json()}
    
    # Validate required fields exist
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${user}    id
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${user}    email
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${user}    created_at
    
    # Validate field values
    ${id}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    id
    Should Be True    ${id} == 123
    
    ${email}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    email
    Should Match Regexp    ${email}    ^[\w\.-]+@[\w\.-]+\.\w+$
```

### Configuration Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate App Config
    ${config}    Load JSON File    config.json
    
    # Required settings
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${config}    database_url
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${config}    api_key
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${config}    timeout
    
    # Validate timeout is reasonable
    ${timeout}    Get From Dictionary    ${config}    timeout
    Should Be True    ${timeout} >= 10 and ${timeout} <= 300
```

### Database Record Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate User Record
    ${user}    Query Database Row    SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=1
    
    ${status}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    status
    Should Be Equal    ${status}    active
    
    ${age}       Get From Dictionary    ${user}    age
    Should Be True    ${age} >= 18
    
    ${role}      Get From Dictionary    ${user}    role
    Should Be Equal    ${role}    admin
```

### Form Data Validation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Registration Form
    ${form_data}    Create Dictionary
    ...    username=testuser
    ...    password=P@ssw0rd!
    ...    email=test@example.com
    ...    age=25
    ...    terms_accepted=True
    
    # Validate username
    ${username}    Get From Dictionary    ${form_data}    username
    Should Be True    len('${username}') >= 3
    
    # Validate password strength
    ${password}    Get From Dictionary    ${form_data}    password
    Should Be True    len('${password}') >= 8
    
    # Validate age
    ${age}    Get From Dictionary    ${form_data}    age
    Should Be True    ${age} >= 18
    
    # Validate terms accepted
    ${terms}    Get From Dictionary    ${form_data}    terms_accepted
    Should Be True    ${terms}
```

## Advanced Dictionary Operations

### Modifying Dictionaries

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Update User Data
    ${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30
    
    # Add new field
    Set To Dictionary    ${user}    role    admin
    
    # Update existing field
    Set To Dictionary    ${user}    age    31
    
    ${age}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    age
    Should Be Equal    ${age}    ${31}
```

### Iterating Over Dictionaries

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate All Fields
    ${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    role=admin
    
    @{keys}    Get Dictionary Keys    ${user}
    FOR    ${key}    IN    @{keys}
        ${value}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    ${key}
        Should Not Be Empty    ${value}
        Log    ${key}: ${value}
    END
```

### Nested Dictionaries

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Nested Data
    ${user}    Create Dictionary
    ...    name=John
    ...    address=Create Dictionary
    ...        street=123 Main St
    ...        city=New York
    ...        zip=10001
    
    ${address}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    address
    ${city}       Get From Dictionary    ${address}    city
    Should Be Equal    ${city}    New York
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Validate Structure Before Values

```robot
# First check key exists
Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${user}    age

# Then validate value
${age}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    age
Should Be True    ${age} > 18
```

### 2. Use Descriptive Key Names

```robot
# Poor
${data}    Create Dictionary    a=John    b=30    c=admin

# Good
${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    role=admin
```

### 3. Group Related Validation

```robot
*** Keywords ***
Validate User Data
    [Arguments]    ${user}
    ${role}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    role
    Should Be Equal    ${role}    admin
    
    ${age}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    age
    Should Be True    ${age} > 18
    
    ${name}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    name
    Should Not Be Empty    ${name}
```

### 4. Use Default Values for Optional Fields

```robot
${status}    Get From Dictionary    ${user}    status    default=pending
Should Be True    '${status}' in ['active', 'pending', 'inactive']
```

By mastering dictionary operations and validation, you can effectively test structured data from APIs, databases, configurations, and complex application state.

Create dictionaries dynamically using Create Dictionary keyword
Retrieve and validate dictionary values using Get From Dictionary
Apply dictionary validation patterns to structured test data

Nested dictionaries and complex data structures
